sections.title: Will and be going to: planned/likely future
sections.content:
We can use either will or be going to to talk about something that is planned, or something that we think is likely to happen in the future:
• We will study climate change in a later part of the course. (or We are going to study …)
• Where will you stay in Berlin? (or Where are you going to stay …?)
• The south of the city won't be affected by the power cuts. (or … isn't going to be affected …)
We often prefer be going to in informal contexts.

sections.title: Will vs be going to: predictions
sections.content:
We use will rather than be going to to make a prediction based on our opinion or experience:
• Why not come over at the weekend? The children will enjoy seeing you again.
• 'Shall I ask Lamar?' 'No, she won't want to be disturbed.'
We use be going to rather than will when we make a prediction based on some present evidence:
• The sky's gone really dark. There's going to be a storm.
• 'What's the matter with him?' 'It looks like he's going to faint.'

sections.title: Prediction verbs with will
sections.content:
To predict the future we often use will with the following prediction verbs: I bet (informal), I expect, I hope, I imagine, I reckon (informal), I think, I wonder and I'm sure. We also use will in questions about predictions with think and reckon:
• I imagine the stadium will be full for the match on Saturday.
• That cheese smells awful. I bet nobody will eat it.
• When do you think you'll finish work?
• Do you reckon he'll say yes?
Be going to can also be used with these phrases, particularly in informal contexts.

sections.title: Will for decisions now; be going to for prior plans
sections.content:
We use will when we make a decision at the moment of speaking and be going to for decisions about the future that have already been made. Compare:
• I'll pick him up at eight. (an offer; making an arrangement now) and
• I'm going to collect the children at eight. (this was previously arranged)
• 'Pineapples are on special offer this week.' 'In that case, I'll buy two.' and
• When I've saved up enough money, I'm going to buy a smartphone.
However, in a formal style, we use will rather than be going to to talk about future events that have been previously arranged in some detail. Compare:
• Are you going to talk at the meeting tonight? and
• The meeting will begin at 9 am. Refreshments will be available from 8:30 onwards.

sections.title: Will and be going to in if-sentences
sections.content:
We can use will or be going to with little difference in meaning in the main clause of an if-sentence when we say that something is conditional on something else:
• You'll / You're going to knock that glass over if you're not careful.
When the future event does not depend on the action described in the if-clause, we use be going to, not will. This kind is mainly found in spoken English. Compare:
• I'm going to open a bottle of lemonade, if you want some. (= I'm going to open a bottle of lemonade. Do you want some?) and
• I'll open a bottle of lemonade if you want some. (= If you say you want some, I'll open it.)
However, we use will, not be going to, when the main clause refers to offers, requests, promises, etc. and ability:
• If Erik phones, I'll let you know. (= an offer)
• If you look to your left, you'll see the lake. (= you'll be able to see)
And when one thing is the logical consequence of another:
• If you don't switch on the monitor first, the computer won't come on.

exercises.question: Have you seen Nadia recently? She'll have another baby.
options: Should be 'is going to have' (present evidence)
exercises.hint: Present evidence (she's visibly pregnant) → use 'be going to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'is going to have' (present evidence)
Present evidence (she's visibly pregnant) → use 'be going to'. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: The method is quite simple, and I'm sure it will be familiar to most of you.
exercises.hint: Prediction based on opinion with 'I'm sure' → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct — prediction based on opinion
Prediction based on opinion with 'I'm sure' → will.

exercises.question: B: I'll see you tomorrow evening, then.
exercises.hint: Decision made at the moment of speaking → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct — decision now
Decision made at the moment of speaking → will.

exercises.question: A: The phone is ringing! B: I ___ (get) it!
exercises.hint: Spontaneous decision made at the moment of speaking → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I'll get it
When a decision is made at the moment of speaking in response to a situation, use 'will' (or 'll). This is not a plan made in advance — it's an on-the-spot response.

exercises.question: Are these new skis yours? Will you take up skiing?
options: Should be 'Are you going to take up' (prior plan)
exercises.hint: Asking about a previously decided plan → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'Are you going to take up' (prior plan)
We use going to here for planned intentions or predictions based on evidence.
💡 Asking about a previously decided plan → be going to.

exercises.question: Wherever you go in Brazil, you'll find the people very friendly.
exercises.hint: General prediction based on experience → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct — prediction based on opinion
General prediction based on experience → will.

exercises.question: Jamie says he'll be a politician when he grows up.
options: Should be 'is going to be' (stated prior intention)
exercises.hint: Jamie already intends this — it's a prior plan → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'is going to be' (stated prior intention)
Jamie already intends this — it's a prior plan → be going to. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: Look at those dark clouds. It ___ (rain).
exercises.hint: Prediction based on present evidence (the clouds) → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is going to rain
When a prediction is based on present visible evidence, use 'be going to'. The clouds are the present evidence that leads directly to the prediction. 'Will' would suggest a general opinion without evidence.

exercises.question: It's getting very humid — we'll have a thunderstorm.
options: Should be 'are going to have' (present evidence)
exercises.hint: Observable evidence (humid air) → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'are going to have' (present evidence)
Observable evidence (humid air) → be going to. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: I hear you'll sell your car. How much do you want for it?
options: Should be 'you're going to sell' (prior decision)
exercises.hint: A prior decision already made → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'you're going to sell' (prior decision)
We use going to here for planned intentions or predictions based on evidence.
💡 A prior decision already made → be going to.

exercises.question: No, I forgot all about them. I'll book them tomorrow.
exercises.hint: Decision made at the moment of speaking → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct — spontaneous decision now
Decision made at the moment of speaking → will.

exercises.question: We ___ (get married) in June — we've already booked the venue.
exercises.hint: Fixed future arrangement (venue booked) → present continuous or be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are getting married / are going to get married
Both work here. The present continuous is preferred for fixed arrangements with concrete plans (venue booked). 'Be going to' expresses intention. 'Will' would sound like a spontaneous decision.

exercises.question: What are those bricks for? I'll build a wall at the side of the garden.
options: Should be 'I'm going to build' (prior plan)
exercises.hint: The bricks are already bought — it's a prior plan → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Should be 'I'm going to build' (prior plan)
We use going to here for planned intentions or predictions based on evidence.
💡 The bricks are already bought — it's a prior plan → be going to.

exercises.question: If you want me to, I ___ how the equipment works.
options: will explain / am going to explain
exercises.hint: Offer in if-sentence: both will and be going to are possible, but will for offer.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will explain / am going to explain
Offer in if-sentence: both will and be going to are possible, but will for offer. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: You ___ your back if you try to lift that box.
options: will hurt / are going to hurt
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will hurt / are going to hurt
Conditional consequence: both are possible. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: If you press the red button, the machine ___.
options: will stop / is going to stop
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will stop / is going to stop
Logical consequence: both are possible. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: If you listen carefully, you ___ an owl in the trees over there.
options: will hear / are going to hear
exercises.hint: Refers to ability → use will, not be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will hear only (ability)
Refers to ability → use will, not be going to. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).
